knowledge_to_learn · agents

Developing agents

Eight chapters and seven exercises, built on one sentence: an agent is a pipeline driver whose next step is chosen by a model at run time instead of by a DAG you wrote in advance. Every hard problem in the field is a consequence of that trade — and every chapter here is one of those consequences.

The ladder the first two chapters climb: transformer — a function, tokens to a next-token distribution → LLM — that function trained, so it carries knowledge and follows instructions → agent — that LLM in a loop, holding tools, pointed at a goal.

What the trade costs, and what each remaining chapter repairs: you can no longer reason about a run before it happens (evals), the model's only state is its context window (context), it knows nothing after its cutoff (knowledge), and it acts on real systems (permissions).

The chapters

Read in order — each is a prerequisite for the next. Pair each with its exercise before moving on.

00 · done

Overview — Transformer → LLM → Agent: the map

The three layers and what each one adds. Where a model's information actually comes from: the weights, and the context. Nothing else feeds a prediction.

01 · done

Transformer — representation, self-attention, architecture

Part 0: raising dimension makes a problem separable, lowering it makes the answer reusable — and the narrow layer is a latent space. Part 1: content-based routing. Part 2: the full architecture.

02 · done

LLM — what training added

Pretraining creates capability; post-training creates behaviour. Which stage is responsible for instruction-following, for tool-calling, for staying on task — because the fix differs depending on the answer.

03 · done

Agent — the loop, and why tools are just text

What crosses the wire on a tool call, who owns the state, and where the halt lives. The eighty-line agent, the five things that break, and the four build shapes on the harness × deployment grid.

04 · done

Context — the window is the whole state

Compaction, tool-result shaping, and the failure modes that make a long run degrade. The chapter that decides whether an agent survives thirty steps or five.

05 · done

Knowledge — giving an agent what it never trained on

Chunking, embeddings vs BM25, reranking, provenance. The question to settle first: whether a vector store beats an agent with grep over a well-structured index — often it does not.

06 · done

Multi-agent — one agent or many

When a planner plus workers plus a critic earns its cost, and when it only multiplies coordination failure. Decided on evidence, which may yet demote this to a section of 04.

07 · done

Evaluation — what counts as "it worked"

Repeats, variance, baselines, cost per completed task, and attributing credit between model, scaffold and tool. An agent without an eval is a demo.

08

Capstone — FoldClaw, a real project

Everything above, applied to a 3D-genomics agent with two papers attached. Not an exercise: it has a corpus, a strategy, and a claim that has to survive review.

The exercises

Each isolates one mechanism, runs on the Mac, and finishes in a sitting. They build on each other — p1's agent is what p3 stresses and p7 measures.

#ExerciseTeachesDone when
p1the 80-line agentthe loop is yours, not the model'sit calls a real tool instead of guessing, and you can point at the line that halts it
p2tool surface designschemas, validation, errors as dataa malformed call returns a useful error and the agent recovers instead of dying
p3context engineeringcompaction, observation shapingyou measure a long run failing, fix it by shaping what the tools return, and measure the difference
p4a knowledge basechunking, retrieval, provenanceretrieval beats a grep-over-index baseline on real questions — or you admit it does not
p5subagentsdelegation and its costyou have one task where delegation wins and one where it loses, with numbers
p6the Claude Agent SDKhooks, permissions, built-in toolsa hook provably blocks an action you decided is forbidden
p7an eval harnessrepeats, variance, baselinesone table comparing two agent variants on the same cases, with variance reported

Why the exercises use a real corpus. p1, p2 and p4 build their tools over FoldClaw's existing knowledge_base/ — 201 paper PDFs, 50 cloned repos and an INDEX.md, already on disk and needing no server. So the first tool you write is a component the capstone keeps, and the throwaway-toy stage is skipped entirely.

How to work through it

  1. Read the chapter, then take its acceptance test. Each one ends with a concrete claim about what you can now do. rc=0 is not understanding — if the test is uncomfortable, the chapter has not landed yet.
  2. Build the paired exercise before moving on. The chapters are short because the exercises carry half the teaching; reading all seven and building none leaves you able to discuss agents and unable to write one.
  3. One session per chapter. 04 and 05 are worth two apiece. If a chapter runs to a third, it has stopped being orientation — note the open question and keep going.
  4. Scaffold FoldClaw's repo after p2, not after p7. By then you will know enough to lay out the project and wire one pipeline stage, and the remaining chapters land on something that already exists. A course is exactly the kind of work that feels like progress while the real project sits still.

On the research in research/raw/: those files are a second model's web search, kept for audit — not findings. A claim there is worth nothing until its cited source has been checked, and the [unverified] markers stay visible in the chapter notes until someone verifies them. Two have been checked so far; the rest have not.
